recipes.name: nmap ping sweep
recipes.what: Find live hosts with ping (ICMP echo) and TCP connection probes, without scanning ports.
recipes.when: First step on a new subnet.
recipes.notes: -sn: find hosts only, skip the port scan. -PE: ping (ICMP echo). -PS/-PA: send TCP probes that start a connection (SYN) or acknowledge one (ACK) on the listed ports. On your own local network nmap uses ARP (address lookups) automatically.

recipes.name: ARP scan
recipes.what: Sweep a range on your own network segment and list each IP address, hardware (MAC) address and vendor.
recipes.when: The target range is on the box's own local network segment, where this is the most reliable discovery.
recipes.notes: --interface: which network card to use. --retry=2: try each address up to two times. The range is the engagement range you enter, not --localnet, which could reach past scope.

recipes.name: List targets (sends no probes)
recipes.what: Expand a CIDR range (an address block like 10.0.0.0/24) and look up names without touching the targets.
recipes.when: Sanity-check scope before scanning.
recipes.notes: -sL: only list targets; it sends name lookups (DNS queries) and nothing to the targets. -R: always do reverse lookups (address to name).

recipes.name: fping sweep
recipes.what: Fast ping sweep that prints only the hosts that answer.
recipes.when: Quick list of live hosts to feed other tools.
recipes.notes: -a: show only hosts that are alive. -g: generate the addresses from a CIDR range (an address block).

recipes.name: netdiscover passive listen
recipes.what: Listen for ARP traffic (address lookups on the local network) to learn hosts without sending anything.
recipes.when: Quiet mapping of a network segment.
recipes.notes: -p: passive mode, sends no ARP requests. -P: print in a script-friendly format. timeout ends the run after the set seconds.

recipes.name: Quick scan of the top 100 TCP ports
recipes.what: Fast scan of nmap's 100 most common TCP ports.
recipes.when: Fast first look at a host or small range.
recipes.notes: -F: fast mode, top 100 ports only. --open: show only open ports. -T4: faster timing.

recipes.name: Top 1000 TCP ports (half-open scan)
recipes.what: nmap's default half-open scan of the 1000 most common TCP ports.
recipes.when: Standard scan after finding live hosts.
recipes.notes: -sS: half-open scan (starts a connection but never finishes it). The default port list is the top 1000.

recipes.name: All 65535 TCP ports
recipes.what: Scan every TCP port on one host.
recipes.when: Thorough follow-up on a single host.
recipes.notes: -p-: all ports. --min-rate 1000: send at least 1000 packets per second (lower it on fragile links).

recipes.name: Top 100 UDP ports
recipes.what: Scan the 100 most common UDP ports.
recipes.when: Looking for DNS (name lookups), SNMP (network device monitoring), NTP (time sync), TFTP (simple file transfer) and similar.
recipes.notes: UDP scans are slow. Results marked open|filtered stay uncertain until you run version detection (-sV).

recipes.name: Low-and-slow half-open scan
recipes.what: Half-open scan with gentle timing and few retries to keep noise down.
recipes.when: Fragile devices or networks that react to fast scans.
recipes.notes: -T2: polite timing. --scan-delay: pause between probes. -Pn: skip the check that the host is up.

recipes.name: TCP connect scan (no root needed)
recipes.what: Scan by making full connections, so it works without administrator rights.
recipes.when: Running without root.
recipes.notes: -sT: complete full connections using the operating system. It shows up in target logs more than the half-open scan (-sS).

recipes.name: Version detection on open ports
recipes.what: Probe open ports to identify the service and its version.
recipes.when: After a port scan, using the open ports it found.
recipes.notes: -sV: detect service versions. --version-intensity 5: how hard to probe, on a 0 to 9 scale (the default is 7).

recipes.name: Operating system guess
recipes.what: Guess the operating system from how its network stack responds.
recipes.when: You need to know what operating system a host runs.
recipes.notes: -O: detect the operating system. --osscan-guess: give a best guess when unsure. Works best with at least one open and one closed port in the list.

recipes.name: Aggressive scan (-A)
recipes.what: Run version detection, OS guess, default scripts and route tracing in one pass.
recipes.when: A deep first pass on a single host.
recipes.notes: -A: shorthand for -sV (versions), -O (operating system), -sC (default scripts) and --traceroute (map the network route).

recipes.name: Default scripts
recipes.what: Run nmap's built-in default scripts (NSE) on chosen ports.
recipes.when: Cheap extra information after a port scan.
recipes.notes: -sC: same as --script=default, the standard set of nmap scripts.

recipes.name: Safe scripts
recipes.what: Run nmap's built-in scripts in the non-intrusive 'safe' group.
recipes.when: Extra enumeration with low impact.
recipes.notes: Scripts in the 'safe' group should not crash services or exploit anything. -sV: detect service versions first.

recipes.name: Discovery scripts
recipes.what: Run nmap's built-in scripts that gather network and service details.
recipes.when: Learn more about network and service details.
recipes.notes: Some scripts send many queries (DNS, SMB file sharing, HTTP), so keep the port list short. -sV: detect service versions.

recipes.name: Vulnerability-check scripts (flagged)
recipes.what: Run nmap's built-in checks for known vulnerabilities; some are intrusive and can upset fragile services.
recipes.when: Lab targets where you accept active checks.
recipes.notes: The vuln group includes intrusive checks, such as tests that can cause denial of service. Use only on lab hosts you are fine disturbing; it checks and does not exploit. For a gentler pass use Safe scripts.

recipes.name: WhatWeb fingerprint
recipes.what: Identify the web server, CMS (content management system), frameworks and headers.
recipes.when: First look at any web (http or https) service.
recipes.notes: -a 1: aggression level 1, a single request. -a 3: level 3, probes more.

recipes.name: Response headers
recipes.what: Fetch the response headers to see the server banner and security headers.
recipes.when: Check the server banner, redirects, HSTS and CSP (browser security policies).
recipes.notes: -s: quiet. -k: ignore certificate errors. -I: ask for headers only. It does not follow redirects, so it never leaves the host you entered.

recipes.name: robots.txt and sitemap
recipes.what: Download robots.txt and sitemap.xml.
recipes.when: Content hints before any directory discovery.
recipes.notes: Enter the URL without a trailing slash. The files may be empty or a 404 (not found) page.

recipes.name: nikto scan
recipes.what: Check for common web misconfigurations and outdated components.
recipes.when: Lab web target where scanner traffic is fine.
recipes.notes: Noisy: it sends many requests. -h: target. -o and -Format txt: save results as plain text.

recipes.name: feroxbuster content discovery
recipes.what: Recursively find hidden directories and files.
recipes.when: Mapping the visible paths of a web app.
recipes.notes: -k: skip certificate checks. -t 20: 20 parallel threads. -d 2: go two directory levels deep.

recipes.name: gobuster directory discovery
recipes.what: Find directories using a chosen wordlist.
recipes.when: Alternative to feroxbuster.
recipes.notes: dir: directory mode. -k: skip certificate checks. -t 20: 20 parallel threads.

recipes.name: testssl encryption audit
recipes.what: Test TLS (web encryption) protocols, ciphers, the certificate and known TLS flaws.
recipes.when: Any HTTPS or other TLS-protected service.
recipes.notes: Kali installs it as testssl. --quiet: less console output.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: SMB info scripts
recipes.what: Query the OS, SMB (Windows file sharing) versions and signing without credentials.
recipes.when: Port 445 or 139 is open.
recipes.notes: Informational scripts only. -p139,445: scan only those two ports.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: NetExec SMB sweep
recipes.what: Show hostnames, domain, OS and SMB (Windows file sharing) signing across a range.
recipes.when: Mapping the Windows hosts on a network.
recipes.notes: No credentials used. NetExec is also installed as nxc. --log: save output to a file.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: Share list (null session)
recipes.what: List SMB (Windows file sharing) shares anonymously.
recipes.when: Check whether a null session (login with no username or password) lists shares.
recipes.notes: -L: list shares. -N: no password. A refusal is a useful result.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: NetExec null-session shares
recipes.what: Check shares across a range using a null session (login with no username or password).
recipes.when: Cross-check the smbclient result on many hosts.
recipes.notes: Empty user and password, one attempt per host. Not a password spray or a guessing attack.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: enum4linux-ng
recipes.what: List users, groups, shares and policy from a Windows host without logging in, using SMB (file sharing), RPC (remote procedure calls) and LDAP (directory lookups).
recipes.when: Windows host with SMB or RPC reachable.
recipes.notes: -A: run all the basic checks. -oA: write results as JSON and YAML files.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: LDAP anonymous rootDSE
recipes.what: Read the LDAP (directory lookup) rootDSE anonymously for naming contexts and domain controller details.
recipes.when: Ports 389 or 3268 are open and you need to identify the domain.
recipes.cmd: ldapsearch -x -H ldap://{host} -s base -b '' -LLL namingContexts defaultNamingContext dnsHostName domainFunctionality | tee {outdir}/ldap-rootdse.txt
recipes.notes: -x: anonymous simple login. -s base -b '': search only the empty root entry, which returns the rootDSE.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: rpcclient null session
recipes.what: Query server and domain info over RPC (remote procedure calls) with no credentials.
recipes.when: Port 445 or 135 is reachable.
recipes.notes: -U '' -N: anonymous login with no password. Most modern hosts refuse it.

recipes.category: Windows file sharing and Active Directory
recipes.name: NetBIOS name scan
recipes.what: Get NetBIOS names (older Windows computer names) across a range.
recipes.when: Quick name mapping on older Windows networks.
recipes.notes: -r: use local UDP port 137 (needs root).

recipes.name: Core record lookup
recipes.what: Ask a lab DNS server for its A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT and SOA records (addresses, mail servers, name servers, text and zone authority).
recipes.when: Starting with a lab domain.
recipes.cmd: for t in A AAAA MX NS TXT SOA; do dig @{host} +noall +answer {domain} $t; done | tee {outdir}/dns-records.txt
recipes.notes: The host is the lab DNS server. +noall +answer: print only the answers.

recipes.name: Zone transfer attempt
recipes.what: Try an AXFR (zone transfer, a full copy of the domain's records) against the lab DNS server.
recipes.when: Lab domain where transfer testing is allowed.
recipes.notes: A refusal is the expected answer from a healthy server.

recipes.name: dnsrecon standard scan
recipes.what: Collect standard DNS records and test for a zone transfer against the lab DNS server.
recipes.when: Domain recon in one tool.
recipes.notes: -d: the domain. -n: use the lab host as the name server. -t std: standard checks, including a zone transfer attempt. -j: save as JSON.

recipes.name: Reverse lookups for a range
recipes.what: Look up the name for every address in a range (PTR, or reverse, lookups).
recipes.when: Mapping names on an internal range.
recipes.notes: -sL: only list targets. -R: always do reverse lookups. Sends name queries only, and only to your own resolver.

recipes.name: snmpwalk with the public community
recipes.what: Walk the device's full SNMP (network device monitoring) data using the default 'public' community string.
recipes.when: The host answers SNMP version 1 or 2c.
recipes.notes: Output is large. Try -v1 if -v2c times out. Tries one default login only; not a guessing attack.

recipes.name: SNMP info scripts
recipes.what: Pull the system description and device info using SNMP (network device monitoring).
recipes.when: UDP port 161 is open.
recipes.notes: -sU: scan UDP. -p161: only the SNMP port. Uses default community strings (SNMP passwords) only.

recipes.name: ssh-audit
recipes.what: Audit the SSH banner, key exchange, ciphers and host keys.
recipes.when: An SSH port is open.
recipes.notes: Protocol negotiation only, no login attempts. -p: the port to check.

recipes.name: FTP anonymous check
recipes.what: Check whether anonymous FTP (file transfer) login is allowed.
recipes.when: Port 21 is open.
recipes.notes: The ftp-anon script tries the anonymous user once. -sV: detect service versions.

recipes.name: RDP security and NTLM info
recipes.what: Show the encryption and security layers of RDP (Windows Remote Desktop) and host details from NTLM (Windows login protocol).
recipes.when: Port 3389 is open.
recipes.notes: rdp-ntlm-info shows the hostname and domain without credentials.

recipes.name: VNC info
recipes.what: Identify the VNC (remote screen sharing) version and login types.
recipes.when: Ports in the 5900 range are open.
recipes.notes: Enter the VNC ports, for example 5900,5901.

recipes.name: SMTP capabilities
recipes.what: List the commands an SMTP (email sending) server supports, plus NTLM (Windows login) info.
recipes.when: Port 25, 465 or 587 is open.
recipes.notes: Does not enumerate users.

recipes.name: iw scan
recipes.what: List nearby access points with channel, signal strength and security.
recipes.when: Quick look without monitor mode (listen-only radio mode).
recipes.notes: Your adapter sends probe requests (normal Wi-Fi scanning). Use airodump-ng or Kismet to stay fully passive.

recipes.name: Start monitor mode
recipes.what: Put the Alfa adapter into monitor mode (listen-only radio mode).
recipes.when: Before airodump-ng or Kismet.
recipes.notes: Usually creates an interface named like wlan0mon. It does not stop NetworkManager (the network connection manager) unless you run 'airmon-ng check kill'.

recipes.name: Stop monitor mode
recipes.what: Return the adapter to managed mode (normal Wi-Fi use).
recipes.when: After a capture.
recipes.notes: Give the monitor interface name.

recipes.name: airodump-ng, all channels
recipes.what: Passively survey access points and clients on the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands.
recipes.when: Wi-Fi site survey.
recipes.notes: --band abg: cover both bands. --output-format csv,pcap: save a spreadsheet file and a packet capture file. -w: the output file name prefix.

recipes.name: airodump-ng, one channel
recipes.what: Capture a single channel to get full coverage of it.
recipes.when: Focus on one access point's channel.
recipes.notes: -c: lock to one channel. --output-format csv,pcap: save a spreadsheet file and a packet capture file.

recipes.name: Kismet survey
recipes.what: Run Kismet on the monitor interface for a set time, logging location if gpsd (the GPS service) has a fix.
recipes.when: Longer survey or wardrive, with the web interface.
recipes.notes: -c: the capture source. -p: log folder. -t: log title. The web interface is at http://localhost:2501.

recipes.name: bluetoothctl scan
recipes.what: Scan for nearby classic Bluetooth and BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) devices.
recipes.when: First Bluetooth survey.
recipes.notes: Uses the default adapter; btmgmt lets you pick another one. --timeout: how many seconds to scan.

recipes.name: btmgmt find
recipes.what: Search for classic Bluetooth devices and BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) devices, with signal strength and flags.
recipes.when: Alternative scan on a chosen adapter.
recipes.notes: --index: which adapter to use. Add -l for BLE only, or -b for classic only.

recipes.name: Classic inquiry (hcitool)
recipes.what: Search for classic Bluetooth devices and list their names.
recipes.when: Fallback; hcitool is deprecated (outdated).
recipes.notes: May be missing on newer installs; prefer bluetoothctl or btmgmt. -i: which adapter. --flush: clear cached results.

recipes.name: BLE scan (hcitool)
recipes.what: Scan for BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) advertisements, the short broadcasts devices send.
recipes.when: Fallback; hcitool is deprecated (outdated).
recipes.notes: Add --duplicates to see repeated advertisements. -i: which adapter.

recipes.name: Bluetooth service browse (SDP)
recipes.what: List the services a classic Bluetooth device offers, using SDP (service discovery).
recipes.when: After finding a classic Bluetooth device you own.
recipes.notes: Connects to the device, so it must be on your Known devices list. sdptool is deprecated (outdated).

recipes.name: Read a device's GATT data
recipes.what: Connect and list a BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) device's GATT services (the list of data it exposes).
recipes.when: Inspect one BLE device you own.
recipes.cmd:
(printf 'connect %s
' {bdaddr}; sleep 8; printf 'menu gatt
list-attributes %s
back
disconnect %s
quit
' {bdaddr} {bdaddr}; sleep 2) | bluetoothctl | tee {outdir}/gatt.txt
recipes.notes: Read-only listing; it fails if pairing is required. Never writes anything to the device.

recipes.name: Bluetooth adapter capture (btmon)
recipes.what: Capture all HCI traffic (the messages between the computer and its Bluetooth adapter) to a btsnoop file.
recipes.when: Debugging scans and connections.
recipes.notes: -w: write to a file. Open the btsnoop file in Wireshark.

recipes.name: Sniffle advertising capture
recipes.what: Sniff BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) advertisements into a pcap (packet capture file) with the CC2652P dongle.
recipes.when: BLE survey without connecting.
recipes.notes: -a: advertising only. -o: write a pcap. Add -c 37|38|39 to pin one channel, or -e for extended advertisements. Assumes the dongle is /dev/ttyUSB0 and Sniffle is in /opt/sniffle (setup puts it there); check with ls /dev/ttyUSB*.

recipes.name: Sniffle one device
recipes.what: Capture advertisements from one device's address.
recipes.when: Follow a specific beacon.
recipes.notes: -m: only this device's MAC (hardware) address. Add -r -70 to drop weak signals. Assumes the dongle is /dev/ttyUSB0 and Sniffle is in /opt/sniffle (setup puts it there); check with ls /dev/ttyUSB*.

recipes.name: rtl_433 decode
recipes.what: Decode sensor transmissions in the ISM (license-free radio) bands to JSON.
recipes.when: Survey devices on 315, 433, 868 and 915 MHz.
recipes.notes: -f: centre frequency. -T: run time in seconds. -F json:file: save results as JSON.

recipes.name: rtl_power sweep, 400 to 470 MHz
recipes.what: Sweep a wide frequency range and log signal power to a CSV file.
recipes.when: Find active frequencies in the UHF (ultra high frequency) band.
recipes.notes: -f lower:upper:step: the range and step size. -i: seconds to average each pass. -e: exit time. -g: receiver gain.

recipes.name: ADS-B aircraft (readsb)
recipes.what: Receive ADS-B (aircraft position broadcasts) on 1090 MHz.
recipes.when: Aircraft survey.
recipes.notes: Stop the dashboard's plane tracker first if it is using the dongle. --interactive: show a live table.

recipes.name: RTL-SDR health check
recipes.what: Confirm the SDR (software-defined radio) dongle is detected and stable.
recipes.when: Before a capture.
recipes.notes: -t: test the tuner range and gains.

recipes.name: tcpdump rotating capture
recipes.what: Capture packets into rotating pcap (packet capture) files.
recipes.when: Long capture with limited disk use.
recipes.notes: -C 100: 100 MB per file. -W 10: keep 10 files. -nn: no name lookups.

recipes.name: tcpdump one host
recipes.what: Capture traffic to or from one host.
recipes.when: Focused capture during testing.
recipes.notes: The trailing 'host' filter (a BPF packet filter) keeps only that host's traffic. -nn: no name lookups.

recipes.name: tshark rotating capture
recipes.what: Capture with the Wireshark engine into rotating files.
recipes.when: A capture you will open in Wireshark.
recipes.notes: -a duration: stop after that many seconds. -b filesize:102400: start a new file every 100 MB. -b files:10: keep 10 files.

recipes.name: Interfaces and addresses
recipes.what: Show each network interface's addresses and link state.
recipes.when: Baseline before scanning.
recipes.notes: -br: brief output.

recipes.name: Routes and neighbours
recipes.what: Show IPv4 and IPv6 routes and the neighbour tables (ARP address lookups for IPv4, ND for IPv6).
recipes.when: Understand the gateway and nearby hosts.
recipes.cmd: (ip route; ip -6 route; ip neigh) | tee {outdir}/ip-route.txt

recipes.name: NetworkManager status
recipes.what: Show device status and visible Wi-Fi networks.
recipes.when: Check which interfaces are up.
recipes.cmd: (nmcli device status; nmcli device wifi list) | tee {outdir}/nmcli.txt
recipes.notes: The Wi-Fi list triggers a scan. Your adapter sends probe requests (normal Wi-Fi scanning).

recipes.name: USB device tree
recipes.what: List attached USB devices.
recipes.when: Verify the radios are detected.
recipes.notes: -t: tree view with drivers.

recipes.name: Bluetooth adapter info
recipes.what: Show the Bluetooth adapter's state and capabilities.
recipes.when: Before Bluetooth scans.
recipes.notes: Shows the address plus supported and current settings.

recipes.name: GPS fix check
recipes.what: Read a few GPS messages from gpsd (the GPS service).
recipes.when: Before wardriving or Kismet location logging.
recipes.notes: Look for TPV messages (position reports) with mode 2 or 3, which means a 2D or 3D fix.

recipes.name: Default logins: SSH (remote login)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on SSH (remote login) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: FTP (file transfer)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on FTP (file transfer) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: Telnet (old plain-text remote login)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on Telnet (old plain-text remote login) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: Windows file sharing (SMB)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on Windows file sharing (SMB) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. Windows can lock accounts after a few wrong tries; check the lab's lockout setting first. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: Windows Remote Desktop (RDP)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on Windows Remote Desktop (RDP) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. Windows can lock accounts after a few wrong tries; check the lab's lockout setting first. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: MySQL database
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on MySQL database to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: PostgreSQL database
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on PostgreSQL database to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: Microsoft SQL Server database
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on Microsoft SQL Server database to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: VNC (remote screen sharing)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default usernames and passwords on VNC (remote screen sharing) to see if any still work.
recipes.when: To prove a device you own isn't still using its out-of-the-box login.
recipes.notes: Uses the default-credential list from SecLists (falls back to the box's own short list). -t 1: one connection at a time. -W 1: wait a second between tries. -f: stop at the first login that works. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: web page login box (HTTP basic)
recipes.what: Tries factory-default logins on a web page that pops up a browser login box.
recipes.when: A device's web page asks for a username and password in a browser pop-up.
recipes.notes: Only works for the browser pop-up kind of login, not login forms on the page. -s: the port the web page is on. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: web admin pages
recipes.what: Finds web admin pages for routers, printers, cameras and similar, and tries their factory-default logins.
recipes.when: Checking a range for devices that still use their default web admin password.
recipes.notes: nmap recognizes the product from the page and tries that product's known default only. Runs one device and one probe at a time, a second apart. The output names the account that works; the password is hidden.

recipes.name: Default logins: network device monitoring (SNMP)
recipes.what: Tries a dozen common SNMP community strings (the password SNMP uses) such as public and private.
recipes.when: A switch, printer or router answers SNMP (UDP port 161).
recipes.notes: A working 'private' community often means the device's settings can be changed over the network. -w 200: wait 200 milliseconds between tries.

recipes.name: Listen for remotes with the YARD Stick One
recipes.what: Record button presses from key fobs, gate remotes and sensors on one frequency. Receive only.
recipes.when: Press your remote near the box while this runs; each press is saved so the dashboard can show it.
recipes.notes: Common frequencies: 315 (US cars, garages), 390 (garage doors), 433.92 (most remotes, sensors). The YARD Stick covers 300-348, 391-464 and 782-928 MHz. Stop any dashboard sub-GHz scan first; only one program can use it at a time. Replaying a capture is a dashboard step for remotes on your Known devices list.

recipes.name: Listen for remotes with the Flipper Zero
recipes.what: Use the Flipper as a backup sub-GHz receiver over USB and record what it hears on one frequency.
recipes.when: When the YARD Stick is busy or unplugged.
recipes.notes: Close qFlipper and the Flipper's own sub-GHz app first. The Flipper usually shows up as /dev/ttyACM0.

recipes.name: Decode sensors on 315, 433 and 915 MHz in turn
recipes.what: Hop the SDR between the three common license-free bands and decode weather stations, tire sensors, doorbells and alarms.
recipes.when: See which sensors are around, without picking a frequency.
recipes.notes: -H 20: stay 20 seconds on each frequency before hopping.

recipes.name: Who's talking on GMRS, FRS, MURS and the ham bands
recipes.what: Sweep the two-way radio bands with the SDR and list channels that are busy, named where they match a known channel.
recipes.when: Check radio activity at a site or event.
recipes.notes: Receive only. Bands: FRS/GMRS, MURS, NOAA weather, 2 m and 70 cm ham.

recipes.name: Hear APRS stations (144.390 MHz)
recipes.what: Decode APRS, the ham radio position and message broadcast, and list stations heard.
recipes.when: See nearby ham stations, weather stations and trackers.
recipes.notes: Give it at least 2 minutes; stations send every few minutes.

recipes.name: Listen to NOAA weather radio
recipes.what: Record a NOAA weather broadcast to a sound file you can play back.
recipes.when: Check the SDR and antenna with a strong, always-on signal.
recipes.cmd: timeout {seconds} rtl_fm -f 162.55M -M fm -s 22050 -g 40 | sox -t raw -r 22050 -e signed -b 16 -c 1 - {outdir}/noaa.wav
recipes.notes: 162.55 MHz is WX7; Tampa Bay is usually 162.55 or 162.475. Change -f if it's quiet.

recipes.name: Wi-Fi survey from the ESP32 Marauder
recipes.what: Have the Marauder list nearby Wi-Fi networks over USB, so the box's own Wi-Fi card stays free.
recipes.when: Second opinion on Wi-Fi, or when the Alfa is busy.
recipes.notes: Listens to beacons only. The Marauder usually shows up as /dev/ttyUSB0.

recipes.name: Meshtastic nodes heard
recipes.what: Show the LoRa mesh nodes the box's Heltec radio has heard, with signal and last seen.
recipes.when: Check the mesh link to your phone, or see who else is on the mesh.
recipes.notes: Reads the bridge's saved list; it doesn't touch the radio.

recipes.name: Log GPS positions
recipes.what: Record the GPS position stream to a file for the set time.
recipes.when: Track where a survey or drive happened.
recipes.notes: Lines with "class":"TPV" carry the position. No fix indoors; put the antenna near a window.

recipes.name: Is the GPS working?
recipes.what: Show the GPS receiver, satellites seen and whether it has a fix.
recipes.when: Before a wardrive or survey.
recipes.cmd: (systemctl is-active gpsd; timeout 20 gpspipe -w -n 15 | grep -E '"class":"(DEVICES|SKY|TPV)"') | tee {outdir}/gps-status.txt
recipes.notes: mode 3 in a TPV line means a 3D fix.

recipes.category: Listening on the wire (no packets sent)
recipes.name: Identify devices from their traffic (p0f)
recipes.what: Guess each device's operating system from the traffic it sends, without sending anything.
recipes.when: Plugged into a switch port or mirror; quiet fingerprinting.
recipes.notes: -o: log file. Leave it running a few minutes on a busy network.

recipes.category: Listening on the wire (no packets sent)
recipes.name: List devices by listening to ARP
recipes.what: Build a list of IP and MAC addresses from ARP traffic only.
recipes.when: Find hosts without sending a single packet.
recipes.notes: -p: passive (listen only). -P: plain output.

recipes.category: Listening on the wire (no packets sent)
recipes.name: Spot new IPv6 devices
recipes.what: Print each IPv6 address as it appears on the network.
recipes.when: Networks where devices only talk IPv6 locally.
recipes.notes: From thc-ipv6. Listens for duplicate address detection messages.

recipes.category: Listening on the wire (no packets sent)
recipes.name: Capture name and address broadcasts
recipes.what: Save DHCP, mDNS, LLMNR and NetBIOS broadcasts, which reveal device names and roles.
recipes.when: Early on a new network.
recipes.cmd: tshark -i {iface} -a duration:{seconds} -f "udp port 67 or udp port 68 or udp port 5353 or udp port 5355 or udp port 137 or udp port 138" -w {outdir}/broadcasts.pcapng
recipes.notes: Open the file in Wireshark afterwards.

recipes.category: Listening on the wire (no packets sent)
recipes.name: Which switch and port am I on?
recipes.what: Listen for LLDP and CDP announcements from the switch (name, port, VLAN).
recipes.when: Plugged into a wall jack or switch port.
recipes.cmd: tshark -i {iface} -a duration:{seconds} -f "ether proto 0x88cc or ether host 01:00:0c:cc:cc:cc" -V | tee {outdir}/lldp-cdp.txt
recipes.notes: Switches announce every 30-60 seconds; give it at least 60.

recipes.name: Check a web server for known problems (nuclei)
recipes.what: Look for exposed files, misconfigurations and known technologies, using safe checks only.
recipes.when: After a web server shows up in a port scan.
recipes.notes: Default-login checks are left out here; they're in the Default logins section. -rate-limit: requests per second.

recipes.name: List what a capture contains
recipes.what: Summarise a Wi-Fi capture file from an earlier run: networks, clients and whether a handshake is in it.
recipes.when: After a dashboard handshake capture or airodump run.
recipes.notes: Uses the newest airodump capture in the toolbox folder.

recipes.name: Wireshark (live capture)
recipes.what: Open Wireshark capturing on an interface.
recipes.when: Look at traffic by eye.
recipes.notes: -k: start capturing straight away.

recipes.name: Gqrx (radio spectrum and listening)
recipes.what: Open the spectrum viewer to see and listen to signals with the SDR.
recipes.when: Find a signal by eye before decoding it.
recipes.notes: Stop the dashboard's plane tracker and other SDR jobs first.

recipes.name: Universal Radio Hacker (analyse a remote's signal)
recipes.what: Open URH to record and pick apart sub-GHz signals.
recipes.when: Work out how a remote encodes its button presses.
recipes.notes: Use its Record and Analysis tabs; sending is done from the dashboard only.

recipes.name: Zenmap (nmap with a window)
recipes.what: Open the nmap GUI.
recipes.when: Browse scan results visually.
recipes.notes: Scans you start in Zenmap aren't scope-checked; prefer the toolbox recipes for scanning.

recipes.name: CHIRP (program Baofeng and GMRS radios)
recipes.what: Open CHIRP to read and write channel lists on your handhelds over USB.
recipes.when: Set up your Baofeng DM-32UV or GM-15 radios.
recipes.notes: Plug the programming cable in first.

chains.name: New network triage
chains.what: Box baseline, find hosts, quick port scan, version detection, then fingerprint one web service.

chains.name: Windows host enumeration
chains.what: Unauthenticated enumeration of one Windows or Active Directory (domain) host.

chains.name: Web app first look
chains.what: Fingerprint and map one web service.

chains.name: Lab DNS recon
chains.what: Name records, dnsrecon and a zone transfer check against the lab DNS server.

chains.name: Bluetooth Low Energy survey
chains.what: Check the radios, scan, capture advertisements, then read a device you own.

chains.name: Wi-Fi survey
chains.what: Passive survey with logging; monitor mode is switched off at the end.

chains.name: Radio receive survey
chains.what: Check the software-defined radio, sweep the UHF band, then decode license-free-band sensors.

chains.name: Service deep-dive
chains.what: All TCP ports, versions and OS guess, then safe scripts and common service checks.

chains.name: Default-login check on one device
chains.what: Tries factory-default logins on every common login service of one device, one at a time.

chains.name: Sub-GHz remotes and sensors
chains.what: Hop the common bands for sensors, then listen on 433.92 MHz with the YARD Stick for remotes.

chains.name: Two-way and ham radio activity
chains.what: Busy channels on GMRS/FRS/MURS/ham, then APRS stations heard.

chains.name: Quiet look at a wired network
chains.what: Find out which switch port you're on and who's there, without sending anything.
